examples: I will bring a friend to the party tomorrow.
May I bring my dog to the park?
nuance: 데려오다 means bringing a person or animal toward where the speaker is. Use 데려가다 instead when you take them away from the speaker. For objects you use 가져오다, not 데려오다.
mistakes: Do not use 가져오다 for people; 가져오다 is only for objects.

usage: I took them to the station.
examples: It is raining so I will take you home.
I have to take the child to school.
Can you take me to the airport?
nuance: 데려다주다 means escorting a person to a place as a favor for them. It combines 데리다 with 주다, so the 주다 part shows the action benefits someone else. For only carrying objects, use 가져다주다 instead.
mistakes: Do not use 데려가다 when you mean kindly escorting someone for their sake; 데려다주다 adds the favor meaning.

usage: I went to see the teacher.
examples: I will go visit grandmother this weekend.
If you have a problem, go to the office.
I want to go visit an old friend after a long time.
nuance: 찾아가다 means actively going to see a person or place, often making an effort to reach them. It moves away from the speaker, while 찾아오다 is when someone comes to the speaker. It is warmer than just 가다 because it implies seeking someone out.
mistakes: Use 찾아오다 when the visitor moves toward the speaker instead of away.

examples: Please grant me just one favor.
아이의 부탁을 다 들어줄 수는 없어요.
I cannot grant all of the child's requests.
I listened to my friend's story to the end.
nuance: 들어주다 means accepting and fulfilling someones request or wish as a favor. It also means listening to someone attentively and supportively. The 주다 part shows the action is done for another persons benefit.
mistakes: Plain 듣다 just means to hear; 들어주다 adds the meaning of granting or kindly listening for someone.

usage: Pack or grab a needed item
I took good care of my sibling.
examples: Be sure to take your wallet when you go out.
Mom packed my lunch for me.
Even if you are busy, you must eat properly.
nuance: 챙기다 has two everyday meanings: gathering and packing things you need, and looking after a person warmly. With food it means to make sure someone eats. It is a very common, caring word in daily Korean life.
mistakes: Do not use 들다 (lift) when you mean packing or remembering to bring something; that is 챙기다.

usage: I saw them off to the station.
examples: It is late so I will walk you home.
I walked my girlfriend to the bus stop.
It is not far so you do not have to see me off.
nuance: 바래다주다 means walking a person partway to their destination to send them off kindly. It is warmer and more personal than just saying goodbye at the door. The 주다 ending shows the act is a favor for the other person.
mistakes: Do not confuse 바래다주다 (walk someone off) with 바라다 (to wish); they are different verbs.

examples: Nice to meet you, let me introduce myself.
I am going to give grandfather a New Year greeting.
You must greet the boss first.
nuance: 인사드리다 is the humble, respectful form of 인사하다, used when greeting someone older or of higher status. The 드리다 ending lowers yourself to honor the listener. Use plain 인사하다 with friends or people your own age.
mistakes: Do not use 인사드리다 with close friends; it sounds too formal, so use 인사하다 instead.

examples: If the bags are heavy, I will help you.
어려운 일이 있으면 언제든지 도와드릴 수 있어요.
If you have any trouble, I can help you anytime.
nuance: 도와드리다 is the humble form of 도와주다, used when helping someone older or a customer. The 드리다 ending shows respect toward the person you help. The phrase 무엇을 도와드릴까요? is the standard polite way to offer service.
mistakes: Do not say 도와주다 to a customer or elder when you want to sound polite; use 도와드리다.

usage: I ask the teacher a favor.
examples: I look forward to your kind help.
May I ask you to handle this task?
I know you are busy, but I will ask just once.
nuance: 부탁드리다 is the humble form of 부탁하다, used to politely ask a favor of someone older or in authority. The set phrase 잘 부탁드립니다 is said when starting work or meeting people you will rely on. The 드리다 ending honors the listener.
mistakes: Do not use 부탁하다 with a superior when you want to be polite; 부탁드리다 is the respectful choice.

examples: I made many friends at the new school.
I want to date a good person.
두 사람은 일 년째 사귀고 있어요.
The two have been dating for a year.
nuance: 사귀다 means both making friends and dating someone romantically, and context tells you which. With 친구 it means becoming friends, and with a person it often means being in a relationship. Note the stem keeps ㅟ, so it is written 사귀어요, not 사겨요.
mistakes: Do not write 사겨요; the standard written form is 사귀어요.

usage: I get close with a friend.
I became close with a coworker.
examples: We became close while exercising together.
I want to become close with my classmates quickly.
As time passes, you will naturally become close.
nuance: 친해지다 means growing closer to someone over time, built from 친하다 (to be close) plus the change verb 지다. The 지다 part shows a gradual change of state. It describes the process of a friendship deepening.
mistakes: 친하다 describes a state of already being close, while 친해지다 describes the change of becoming close.

usage: I got along well with new friends.
examples: I often hang out with neighborhood friends.
그 색은 너한테 정말 잘 어울려.
That color really suits you well.
I like mingling with many people.
nuance: 어울리다 has two everyday meanings: mingling and spending time with people, and matching or suiting well. With people it means to get along and hang out, and with clothes or colors it means to look good together. Context makes the meaning clear.
mistakes: Do not use 놀다 (play) in formal situations; 어울리다 is the natural word for socializing and getting along.

usage: I broke up with my boyfriend.
examples: I parted from my friend in front of the station.
We said goodbye late at night.
The two broke up last year.
nuance: 헤어지다 means parting ways after being together, and it is also the standard word for a romantic breakup. With friends it simply means to say goodbye and go separate ways. It is the natural opposite of 만나다.
mistakes: Do not use 떠나다 (leave a place) when you mean two people parting; that is 헤어지다.

usage: I take care of a child.
examples: 부모님이 안 계실 때 동생을 돌봐요.
I take care of my sibling when my parents are away.
Please look after my dog this weekend.
I have to take care of my sick friend.
nuance: 돌보다 means looking after and caring for a person, child, animal, or even a plant over time. It carries warmth and responsibility, more than just watching. With babies and pets it is the everyday word for caregiving.
mistakes: Do not use 보다 (to see) alone for caregiving; 돌보다 means actively caring for someone.
